items.title: The deal closed. When do the savings start?
items.description: Purchasing synergies can materially improve homebuilder acquisition savings and strengthen the economics of the deal. They can also be overstated when the deal model doesn't fully reflect the cost and time required to achieve them. Combining the purchasing volume of two builders should create leverage for better pricing and stronger margins. But before that leverage is real, someone has to determine what each company is buying, how their supplier agreements differ and what it will take to operate under a common set of processes. That's where the financial projections meet the realities of running the business. I've worked on acquisition diligence and integration across different industries, and the question I believe deserves more attention isn't how much a deal can save. It's when those savings actually show up in the P&L. For homebuilders , technology has a significant role in the solution. Buying power only matters if you can use it Consider a builder acquiring a regional operation with established supplier relationships and a healthy pipeline of homes under construction . The opportunity is clear. The combined company is buying more materials across more communities, which should create leverage to negotiate better terms. Now look at what has to happen to capture those savings. The acquired company may use a different ERP, organize its purchasing data differently or have supplier agreements that don't align with the parent company's contracts. Before purchasing leadership can negotiate from a position of combined volume, they need an accurate, combined view of what that volume actually is. Meanwhile, both businesses still have homes to build. Construction schedules can't be put on hold while systems are reconciled. It's entirely possible to have a sound purchasing strategy and spend the first several months after closing working through the operational issues that prevent successful execution. As builders know better than anyone, these delays carry real cost. If the acquisition model assumes purchasing savings will start contributing to margin within two quarters and integration takes a year, you won't get the return you underwrote. The savings may still arrive, but every quarter of delay is value that doesn't come back. This matters even more when interest rates are high. There's usually a second cost hiding in the same delay: running two sets of systems, two sets of processes and often two teams doing the same work until integration is complete. Those dual running costs rarely get the same scrutiny as the synergy number. Homebuilder M&A integration is a financial decision Technology deserves a more prominent place in acquisition diligence and homebuilder M&A integration, particularly when operating efficiencies account for a meaningful share of the expected return. Knowing which applications a company runs is a starting point. The more important question is how those systems will work inside the larger organization, and what it will cost to get them there. Can the acquiring builder get reliable purchasing data across both businesses on day one? Can existing systems exchange the information needed to keep construction moving? What will it cost to maintain separate environments while integration is underway, and for how long? These sound like operating questions. They're also valuation questions. The same applies to proprietary technology . Many builders have invested heavily in systems developed specifically for their businesses, and there can be good reasons for doing so. The challenge arises when those systems must accommodate an organization they weren't originally designed to support. Custom integrations require people and capital to build. They also require ongoing security and maintenance as the business changes, and that cost doesn't end when the integration goes live. I want to understand those costs before committing to an acquisition, not discover them in the first integration budget review. The advantage of an established network One factor that is often overlooked in technology discussions is the value of connectivity that already exists. A homebuilding operation depends on relationships with suppliers, manufacturers and trades that extend well beyond its internal systems. Those connections become particularly important when a company expands into new markets or brings another Builder into the organization. At Hyphen Solutions, we've spent more than 25 years building a network that connects hundreds of Builders and more than 18,000 suppliers, trades and manufacturers across North America. That matters because a builder operating within an established network isn't starting from zero. In many acquisitions, the acquired builder's suppliers are already on the same network as the parent company. When that's the case, many of the connections the combined company needs exist before the deal closes, and purchasing teams aren't onboarding suppliers a second time while homes are under construction. Our technology connects construction scheduling, purchasing and supplier communication, and integrates with different ERP and back-office environments. That gives purchasing leadership the combined view of orders, pricing and supplier activity across both businesses that consolidated buying depends on, without replacing every existing system first. We’ve seen this play out over the past year as a number of builders combined operations, and the ones that moved fastest had something in common. Their companies already shared many of the same suppliers and trades on the Hyphen network. items.title: The mortgage operating model after AI
items.description: In my previous two articles, I explored why the mortgage industry's biggest AI challenge is structural and how the traditional brokerage operating model creates complexity as businesses grow . That brings us to a more fundamental question: If we could redesign mortgage origination around what AI now makes possible, what would we build? Today, the process is organized around a series of narrowly defined roles and handoffs, with loan officers, assistants, processors, underwriters and others each responsible for moving the file to the next stage. Every handoff creates another opportunity for information to get lost and responsibility to be pushed downstream. I believe the mortgage operating model of the future will be organized around a persistent, provable understanding of the borrower and the lifecycle of the loan, rather than the people, systems and handoffs that define the process today. Start with an evidence-based picture of the borrower At its core, a mortgage involves building an evidence-based profile of an individual and applying a risk model to it. Today, that profile is repeatedly reconstructed or revalidated by originators, lenders, underwriters and other participants because each has limited visibility into, or confidence in, the work that came before. Imagine instead a persistent, evidence-backed borrower profile that brings together information from pay stubs, tax returns, credit reports and other sources, with each data point retaining a verifiable connection to its original evidence. That includes where the information came from and how it was calculated, interpreted or reconciled with other information. The result would be a more complete and transparent understanding of the borrower that persists throughout the loan lifecycle. Rather than reconstructing that information each time another party needs to assess the loan, participants could trace the underlying evidence, understand how previous conclusions were reached and build on the work already performed, while still conducting their own necessary evaluations and verifications. Apply different risk models to the same underlying evidence To be sure, understanding the borrower is only part of the equation. Every lender, agency and mortgage product has its own requirements and risk criteria. Today, those requirements are translated into guidelines, matrices and documents that must be interpreted and applied by people across multiple stages of the origination process. With a common, verifiable borrower profile, different risk models could be applied to the same underlying information. A system could evaluate how Fannie Mae , Freddie Mac or a particular lender would assess the borrower, identify missing evidence and determine what needs to happen next. Specialized AI agents could then coordinate and execute much of that work, from collecting documents and preparing calculations to addressing conditions and identifying exceptions that require human review. Consider how often a missing document or unresolved discrepancy surfaces late in the process, forcing a loan officer or processor to revisit work that should have been completed weeks earlier. With a more complete understanding of the borrower and the requirements of the loan, those agents could identify many of those issues earlier, coordinate the necessary follow-up and maintain an auditable record of the work performed. The implications extend beyond making individual tasks faster to changing how information is maintained and how work gets done, creating an opportunity to rethink the organization itself. When the loan carries the context, the organization can change When technology maintains the evidence, context and requirements throughout the loan lifecycle, people no longer need to serve as the connective tissue between every task and system. Specialized AI agents can increasingly handle work traditionally distributed across different roles, while experienced mortgage professionals oversee execution, validate results and exercise judgment. Consider the processor, whose role could evolve from coordinating documents, conditions and handoffs to overseeing the quality and performance of the loan process. Specialized AI agents could collect documents, prepare calculations and track conditions, while the processor sets standards, validates results, resolves exceptions and continuously improves the workflow. This shift would also change how mortgage organizations define and reward expertise. Rather than measuring success by the number of people someone manages or the tasks they complete, organizations could focus on accurate files, predictable closings, borrower experience and ultimately, a lower cost to originate. By reducing manual handoffs and repetitive work, experienced professionals could oversee more loans without a corresponding increase in staffing. The result would be a mortgage organization structured around the lifecycle of the loan rather than inherited job descriptions. Instead of scaling by adding more people to manage each stage of origination, companies could build teams around broader accountability for the loan from application to funding, with AI supporting the work required along the way. What it all means Origination is the logical place to prove this model because it is where the borrower's evidence is first assembled and evaluated. But once a provable, evidence-based profile exists, its usefulness could extend well beyond funding. Other participants across the mortgage value chain, including investors and capital markets firms, could eventually apply their own risk models to the same underlying information, allowing for more granular risk assessment without repeatedly reconstructing the loan. My prediction is that AI will reshape not only mortgage organizations , but also how they work together. items.title: Finance of America grows origination volume but reports $110M loss in Q3
items.description: Finance of America ( FOA ) reported a net loss of $110 million in the third quarter of 2026, as noncash fair value adjustments weighed on results despite growth in the company's home equity lending business. The Plano, Texas-based company on Tuesday reported $748 million in funded volume for the quarter ending Sept. 30, up 24% from $603 million during the same period last year. Year-to-date funded volume reached $2.07 billion, a 17% increase from the first nine months of 2025. FOA recorded a basic loss of $5.24 per share, compared with a loss of 98 cents per share in the third quarter of 2025. The quarterly net loss was primarily driven by $125 million in noncash fair value adjustments. On an adjusted basis, FOA reported net income of $6 million, or 28 cents per share, compared with $33 million, or $1.33 per share, a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA totaled $17 million, down from $55 million in the third quarter of 2025. “The third quarter of 2026 demonstrated the continued strength of our platform, with funded origination volume growing 24% year over year. While higher interest rates drove near-term pressure on earnings , we believe this impact is temporary,” CEO Graham Fleming said in a statement. “We have already taken steps to improve margins.” During the company's earnings call, Fleming said the company remains focused on production growth, operational efficiency and cash generation, and explained that margins compressed after the Federal Reserve shifted from cutting to raising interest rates. "We have already made the necessary changes to product pricing, and we expect margins to return to historical levels in the first half of 2027," Fleming told investors. "Finance of America has grown volumes on average by 20% each year since 2023. The third quarter was a challenging rate environment, with the 10-year Treasury yields increasing over 75 basis points during the quarter, a reaction to the Fed's pivot to raising rates and elevated inflation," he added. Retirement solutions performance FOA’s retirement solutions segment, which originates home equity-based financing products, including reverse mortgages , recorded $748 million in funded volume during the quarter, up 24% year over year. "Our retirement solutions revenue margin was impacted in the third quarter, decreasing to 9%, compared with 11.3% in the third quarter of 2025, and a historical average since the start of 2024 of 10.7%," Fleming said during the call. "We believe these impacts are temporary and do not change the underlying fundamentals of our business." Revenue for the segment totaled $67 million, down 1% from the prior-year period and a decrease from Q2 2026 's $74 million. Pretax income fell to $3 million, down from $10 million a year earlier, while adjusted net income declined to $9 million, down from $20 million. The company attributed the decline in profitability primarily to pressure on origination margins as benchmark interest rates increased during the quarter. It said it implemented product and pricing adjustments to address the impact and expects margins to return to historical levels. For the first nine months of 2026, the retirement solutions segment generated $2.07 billion in funded volume, up 17% year over year. Revenue increased 14% to $208 million. "Since 2023, our submission volumes have increased by 21% annually, while our funded volume has grown by 20% annually. This is across our product suite, as HECM volume is up 14% year over year, HomeSafe first liens are up 15%, and HomeSafe seconds are up 63%," FOA President Kristen Sieffert said during the call. Portfolio management performance FOA's portfolio management segment, which generates revenue through net interest income and fair value changes on portfolio assets, reported a pretax loss of $138 million, compared with an $11 million loss in the third quarter of 2025. The company attributed the loss primarily to negative non-cash fair value adjustments on retained interests in securitizations. Portfolio management reported adjusted net income of $11 million, down from $30 million a year earlier. Assets under management in the segment increased 23% year over year to $37.4 billion. The growth reflected new originations and the acquisition of Onity Mortgage Corp. ‘s HECM servicing portfolio on July 1. For the first nine months of 2026, portfolio management recorded a pretax loss of $128 million, compared with pretax income of $202 million in the same period last year. Adjusted net income totaled $57 million, down from $66 million. FOA ended the third quarter with $118 million in cash and cash equivalents, up from $85 million at the end of June. The company attributed the increase to cash generation from originations and capital markets activity. Total equity stood at $307 million as of Sept. 30, including $259 million attributable to common stock. Book value was $28.08 per common share. The company said it expects to complete a $60 million paydown of senior secured notes in November. Looking ahead to the final quarter of 2026, chief financial officer Matt Engel said the company expects funded volume to reach $3.1 billion to $3.4 billion, a range "supported by consumer demographics , our product breadth, and ongoing conversion improvements." items.title: MSRs trade at richest levels in decades as lenders, funds pile in
items.description: Chicago-based Rate has recently changed its servicing strategy, retaining mortgage servicing rights ( MSRs ) instead of selling. “We've been retaining all of our MSRs for the last 12 months, so we're over $50 billion in MSR retention,” CEO Victor Ciardelli said in an exclusive interview with HousingWire . “We really believe in retaining the MSRs, staying close to the customer.” Rate’s approach reflects a broader trend of mortgage lenders holding onto their portfolios or seeking to add MSRs as a way to recapture borrowers when rates eventually fall. John Sullivan, managing director of MSR advisory services at Milliman , has seen that shift firsthand. Speaking during IMN’s Mortgage Servicing Rights Conference in New York on Monday, he said he’s having more conversations with clients about retaining their portfolios “unless liquidity is an issue,” and about monetizing them if they are not hedging . Higher demand for MSRs is not limited to independent mortgage banks ( IMBs ). Depository institutions are also showing more interest, executives told HousingWire during the conference. “ Banks historically are not great at recapture, but we think that given some changes on the Basel capital front, we're going to see more bank participation in this space on a go-forward basis, and I think banks will think about just customer acquisition in general, cross-selling in general,” said Larry Goldstone, president of capital markets and lending at BSI Financial Services . Strategic investors are also willing to grow their portfolios. Rob Williams, co-founder and CEO at Grander Investment Management , a specialized asset manager focused on MSRs, said he’s tactical but sees MSRs as a “spectacular asset” that can reach double-digit returns. “I can probably be more patient,” he said during the conference, when comparing his approach to the other buyers. “I can be more tactical.” The buyer base views MSRs through different lenses. Rich McRedmond, managing director at CrossCountry Mortgage , said that while banks see MSRs as part of their consumer banking strategy, real estate investment trusts ( REITs ) see them as a pure investment. And mortgage companies see them as a borrower recapture tool “from when they get the mortgage to when they get the next mortgage.” Multiples and yields Conventional, pristine MSRs are seeing 7x multiples amid high demand, a level not reached in more than two decades. “We've seen some pretty extraordinary multiples of late,” Goldstone said. “This is usually an inexpensive asset, and therefore an asset that people want to be able to own. I think you could hedge MSR pretty effectively and still get low-double digits, high-single digit returns up until about the last year. That's pretty attractive for an asset that really doesn't have a whole lot of credit risk associated with it.” Simon Aldrich, senior executive vice president at Freedom Mortgage , believes that at this point, “it’s very difficult to be in this market if you don’t have recapture.” “In our model, we don't hedge, so I'm not worried about rates going up or rates going down. Rates go up, I get the pickup at slower speeds. Rates go down, our call center kicks into gear.” Bayview Asset Management , which acquires MSRs from the bulk and flow markets and uses five different subservicers, has also built out a full recapture strategy, including through its acquisition of Guild Mortgage . Managing director Michael Lau said Bayview has partnered with investors, including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds, that have long-duration strategies. “MSRs are great because they're not correlated to the equity or the bond market , and gives them something alternative that also, because we hedge out all the interest rate risk for them, delivers a very consistent return on their money, net of our fees,” Lau said. Opportunistic sales Some companies have taken advantage of current pricing to sell MSRs for different reasons, including to pay back debt or raise funds. In the third quarter , Rocket Companies sold $23 billion of unpaid principal balance (UPB) for $379 million in cash proceeds, retaining the subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the MSRs sold. Analysts told HousingWire the company usually sells production in the wholesale channel due to lower recapture possibility. Pennymac Financial Services entered into an agreement to sell $29 billion in UPB of low-coupon conventional MSRs, with $490 million of proceeds expected to pay down debt. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter. Meanwhile United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) sold about $60 billion — at a roughly 6x multiple — to JPMorgan Chase , sources told HousingWire. The companies declined to comment. This is part of a plan to bring up to $80 billion of MSRs to market in the fourth quarter, with the expectation of being paid more than $1.8 billion in an attempt to reduce leverage. Newrez President Baron Silverstein said his company is taking a disciplined approach. Across the Newrez portfolio, 60% of loans were originated before or during the COVID-19 pandemic. “In today's market, given where we are from a rate perspective, there's pressure in a competitive environment where MSRs get created — where that gain on sale is from an all-in gain-on-sale perspective on loans that we originate or buy. And when we think about that, we get very selective and stay very disciplined about how we put that capital to work,” Silverstein said. “When you think about hedging in a market like this, that also requires a lot of capital, and it's very challenging in these markets today, regardless of the interest rate environment. items.title: Texas Flips Blue, Putting Data Center Boom On Notice
items.description: Texas elected Democrats to its top offices for the first time in decades, a move that could ripple through the burgeoning data center industry across the state. X/Gina Hinojosa Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico Gina Hinojosa was named the projected winner for Texas governor, and James Talarico was named the projected winner for U.S. Senate on Tuesday night by The Associated Press. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott , the 12-year Republican incumbent, said he called Hinojosa to concede at about 10 p.m. CT Tuesday. Hinojosa had more than 4.4 million votes , or 53%, with 80% of Texas counties reporting late Tuesday, compared to about 3.8 million votes for Abbott. The 52-year-old Austin state representative overcame a 4-1 spending disparity and will become the first Latina governor of Texas. The Texas Republican Party hadn’t lost a gubernatorial election since 1990. For the Texas commercial real estate industry, all eyes will likely turn to Hinojosa’s plan for a data center development moratorium , as well as stricter regulations on water and power usage and an end to tax breaks for the industry. Texas has more data centers under development than any other state, and it rose in the ranks to the top data center market this year, surpassing Virginia. Talarico has also called for tighter data center regulations and said their construction shouldn’t contribute to the state’s affordability crisis . While the Republican candidates had also called for the end of tax breaks and stricter regulations for data center development, their plans differed at the granular level. Talarico’s defeat of the Republican Senate nominee, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton , will make him the state’s first Democratic senator since 1988, before the 37-year-old Talarico was born. Talarico had 4.7 million votes , or about 55%, to Paxton’s 3.7 million late Tuesday night. Paxton, who defeated incumbent John Cornyn in the primary election, faced controversies like his 2023 impeachment and high-profile members of his party refusing to back him . More than a third of the impeachment articles involved Paxton’s relationship with embattled Austin real estate developer Nate Paul . Paxton also has a significant real estate portfolio that is at issue in his ongoing divorce. items.title: Hynes Vows To Bring Property Tax Stability As New Cook County Assessor
items.description: The 2026 Illinois midterms featured a slew of Democratic wins across the ballot as part of sweeping victories for the party across the country. In perhaps the most consequential result for Illinois' commercial real estate investors, Democrat Pat Hynes handily won the race for Cook County assessor , defeating Libertarian challenger Nico Tsatsoulis by a margin of about 85% to 15%. Courtesy of Pat Hynes Pat Hynes Hynes, who unseated two-term incumbent Fritz Kaegi in the March Democratic primary, has promised to make the Assessor's Office "boring again" by being more predictable and accurate. The former Lyons Township assessor plans to create a new department in the Assessor's Office called the Department of Economic Development, which will work with aldermen and mayors to offer transparency in the assessment process for new development. Hynes is the second member of his family to lead the Assessor's Office. His uncle Thomas Hynes held the role from 1979 to 1997. Siegel Jennings partner Molly Phelan told Bisnow on Tuesday that she believes Hynes' win will bring more tax certainty to Cook County — and investors in tow. "I'm very bullish on development in Cook County because we're going to have a new assessor coming in," Phelan said. "I think we're going to have government that understands that we need more taxpayers and more buildings coming in to level out the property tax base." Elsewhere in Illinois, incumbent Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker comfortably secured a third term, capturing about 60% of the vote and defeating Republican challenger Darren Bailey and independent opponent Collin Corbett . Pritzker has been a major backer of the sprawling Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park on the South Side but has taken a more cautious approach to data center development in the state in 2026. Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton made history in her U.S. Senate win, as she will become the sixth Black woman to ever serve in the Senate. Alexi Giannoulias, who is a front-runner in the 2027 Chicago mayoral election, also won his campaign for secretary of state by a margin of 64% to 35%. items.title: Donalds Makes History With Win For Florida Governor, Voters OK Property Tax Amendment
items.description: Florida voters showed up — even as some poll locations were moved due to severe flooding — to elect Byron Donalds as the state’s 47th governor, succeeding Gov. Ron Desantis . Donalds makes history as the Sunshine State's first Black governor. In addition to electing the state’s first new governor in seven years, voters passed a property tax amendment that increases homestead exemptions significantly over the next two years. Bisnow/Chloe Gallivan Donalds won with 50.1% of the vote, a 1.4-percentage-point lead over his opponent, Democrat David Jolly . “As your next governor, we are going to make sure that Florida remains the very best state in all of America,” Donalds said at his watch party at Broward County’s Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Hollywood. “We're going to be focused on the issues that I've been talking about on this campaign trail for a long time. We are going to drive down costs for the people of this state.” Both candidates and their campaigns leaned heavily on their approaches to affordability, a leading issue for Florida, which is experiencing an outflow of middle-class residents citing affordability concerns. The trend is especially evident in South Florida, where an affordable housing crisis is brewing amid an influx of wealthy individuals. Miami-Dade County lost more than 10,000 residents between 2024 and 2025, placing it among the three counties with the nation’s largest population declines, according to the Census Bureau . Donalds, who has spent the last 10 years in Florida politics and serves as the U.S. representative for Florida’s 19th Congressional District, wants to lower homebuilding costs to boost housing inventory. He has called for smaller units from developers, removing zoning restraints, specifically in Miami-Dade County, and promoted the removal of local zoning restraints to boost housing inventory. The new governor-elect, a Florida State University graduate, also supports the state seeking technology to modernize permitting systems. In addition to a focus on affordability, Donalds pushed to expand transparency on healthcare costs and government spending, worked to move NASA’s headquarters and the Space Force Academy to Florida, and focused on early literacy for children. Jolly, a lawyer and former Republican congressman who turned Democrat in 2025, launched his run in June 2025, campaigning on affordability largely through property insurance, calling for state-backed funding to cover hurricane and wind risk with aims to cut premiums by up to 70%. He also supported using state money to invest in workforce and affordable housing and expanding down payment assistance. “The movement we started doesn't go away tomorrow,” Jolly said onstage at the Tampa Convention Center, where he held his watch party. “It exists to hold our leaders accountable.” Donalds’ win keeps Florida’s 28-year red streak alive, even after high expectations for Jolly’s performance, and falls in line with the real estate industry’s preferences . Wikimedia Commons/Gage Skidmore Byron Donalds at AmericaFest 2025 Some of South Florida’s largest commercial real estate investors funneled millions into Donalds’ campaign in recent months. It had amassed more than $150M by Tuesday, according to the Florida Department of State’s campaign finance database . That is a massive lead against the roughly $14M Jolly collected in donations by Election Day. Among the largest donors to Donalds were Citadel founder Ken Griffin , who donated $15M in two separate payments in July and August, and Related Ross head Stephen Ross , who donated $1M, according to the database. Other donors included Related Group , JDS Development ’s Michael Stern , Oak Row Equities and Property Markets Group . Jolly’s campaign landed donations from Compass agent Michelle Howland and Deborah Simon, daughter of Simon Property Group co-founder Melvin Simon. Florida’s new governor will be sworn into office in January. On top of heavy real estate backing, Donalds earned an almost immediate endorsement from President Donald Trump when he announced he was running for governor in February 2025 and later landed DeSantis’ backing . Beyond electing a new governor, voters approved a property tax amendment targeting housing costs, clearing the 60% hurdle to pass. The amendment will raise Florida’s $50K homestead exemption to $150K next year and $250K in 2028 without exempting tax levies for school district properties. Despite touting greater affordability for homeowners, localities have warned that the amendment’s passage could mean multimillion-dollar cuts to their budgets. In response to the measure, the city of Miami prepared a 25% budget cut to local hospitals, police, fire, parks, public schools and water management, which Related Group's Jorge Peréz cautioned could stunt the city’s ability to attract and retain residents. Landlords may carry the weight if municipalities opt to raise taxes on commercial properties to fund the gap. Rental properties that aren’t homesteaded, because they aren’t owner-occupied, could see a rise in property taxes, which could be passed on to renters . “Anytime some commercial businesses get their costs raised, they tend to pass it on to the consumer,” Kaufman Rossin tax principal and leader Ken Rios said. “So talking about affordability for the rental market, if the commercial owners are paying more, they may increase rents and it may impact the consumer.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Byron Donalds , David Jolly , Ron DeSantis

items.title: Developer Picks Up Industrial Site, Plots 1.3M SF Development: The Chicago Deal Sheet
items.description: Logistics Property Co. is making another Midwestern buy, picking up its fourth development site in the Chicago area in the last year. The company closed on a 74-acre site at 23960 S. Houbolt Road in Joliet for an undisclosed price. When the development is complete, the property will total close to 1.3M SF. Unsplash/user user “23960 S Houbolt Road is the premier location for bulk users given the immediate proximity to the intermodal and the new Houbolt Road Extension,” Ben Fish, associate market leader at the company, said in a statement. “We’re excited to continue to grow our Midwest portfolio with this property, our fourth development site in the Chicago market in the last year.” Acquisition of the development site follows the closing of three development properties: 424 Howard Ave. in Des Plaines, 390 O’Hare Logistics Park in Schaumburg, and 2349 W. items.title: Housing Market Feels the Chill as Buyers Pull Back—but Sellers Are Not Panicking Yet
items.description: The national housing market is feeling the chill as high borrowing costs are forcing frustrated buyers to throw in the towel, yet sellers are largely digging in to wait out the slump. Two key metrics— price cuts and delistings —tell the story of American home sellers' resilience in the face of adversity this fall. Across the U.S., about 4.4% of active listings were pulled off the market in October, down from 4.6% a year ago, according to the latest Realtor.com® monthly housing market trends report released on Wednesday. On a monthly basis, the delisting rate has ticked up slightly from 4% in September, in line with typical seasonal trends, but no more than that, even with mortgage rates well exceeding 7% and buyer demand waning. According to Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel , delistings matter because they act as a canary in the coal mine. A jump in the delistings rate could be a sign of a housing market in distress. However, the October findings show that sellers are not ready to take their ball and go home yet. "Job relocations, family circumstances, and financial challenges are among the top reasons I am seeing sellers stay on the market rather than withdraw and wait until spring," Josh Stimpson , a real estate agent at The Realtive Group of Reliant Realty in Nashville, TN, tells Realtor.com. "The rising cost of living is also a major factor, prompting many sellers to seek more affordable housing." Price cuts plateau The other key data point used to assess the strength of the U.S. housing market is price cuts. According to the latest housing market data, much like with delistings, there has not been a dramatic change up or down in the share of listings offering discounts, although it remained elevated. For the fourth consecutive month, more than 1 in 5 active listings (20.5%) saw a price cut, marking the highest October reading since 2022 and the second highest this year, trailing only September, which set a four-year record. However, Krimmel points out that the national price cut rate actually retreated 0.3 percentage points month over month, snapping a nine-month streak of monthly gains. Annually, the share of active listings with price cuts ticked up by just 0.2 percentage points. Sellers "are getting used to not everything selling quickly," Learka Bosnak , an agent with of Heather & Learka Team at Douglas Elliman in Beverly Hills, CA , tells Realtor.com. "They aren’t seeing compelling evidence that a slightly lower price will lead to a quick sale. Plus, they aren't feeling a lot of pressure monthly because so many have low-interest-rate mortgages." Loading... A pause, not a panic Taken together, the October delisting and price cut readouts lead to one conclusion concerning the present state of the market. "Right now, it looks more like a seller pause than an exodus," says Krimmel. "Sellers are disengaging rather than showing signs of distress." Regionally, price reductions remained least common in the systemically undersupplied Northeast (16.8% of listings) and most common in the West (21.9%), with the Midwest and South falling in between at 21% each. Across the 50 largest metro markets, 12 saw price cuts on a quarter or more of the listings, unchanged from September. Thirty-four of the metros are running above their year-ago cut rate, down from 36 in September. At the local level, price discounts in October were most common in Indianapolis (31.8%), Denver (31.3%), and Portland, OR (31.1%). While the delisting and price cut numbers stop short of signaling a panic among sellers, October trends do point to a noticeable pullback. New listings and pending sales slump New listings—a measure of homeowners putting their properties on the market—dropped 9.5% from September and 7.5% from a year ago, marking the steepest decline in more than three years. "Sellers know this is a poor time to list, and you do not list into weak demand unless you need to," notes Krimmel. At the same time, pending sales plunged 10.5% year over year—the biggest annual drop since October 2023. However, active listings jumped 7.4% year over year, topping 1.18 million homes for sale—the fourth consecutive month of accelerated growth. This reflects properties piling up on the market as buyers see their purchasing power diminished by surging 30-year mortgage rates, which averaged 7.33% in October. For context, that is a staggering 107 basis points above October 2025 levels and 53 basis points higher than at the start of September. "Elevated interest rates and ongoing affordability challenges have caused many buyers to pause, and the midterm election may be adding to that hesitation," notes Stimpson. "As a result, showing activity has declined and days on market are rising, particularly in Nashville and the surrounding areas." Silver lining for buyers However, patient buyers willing to stick it out can still find attractive deals and see their negotiating position strengthened. "Buyers can often retain their inspection, appraisal, and financing contingencies while also requesting additional repairs, a longer closing period, or a home warranty," says Stimpson. "Properties with extended market exposure may offer even greater leverage, including opportunities to negotiate a lower purchase price or secure seller concessions." Looking ahead to late fall and winter, the Nashville agent says there are some encouraging signs on the horizon, including gradually easing mortgage rates, closings holding steady in Middle Tennessee , and premium listings continuing to attract multiple offers. Yet, both Stimpson and Bosnak agree that what the market sorely lacks is a sense of certainty. "No one is sure what the market or the world will look like in a year, so it doesn’t feel weird to lean into that wait-and-see part of human nature," says the Beverly Hills agent. items.title: What housing market headlines can't tell your clients
items.description: Mortgage rates are moving closer to 7%, and housing demand is showing signs of stabilizing. But what does that mean for a homeowner preparing to list, a buyer wondering whether to wait or an agent trying to set realistic expectations? In his latest Housing Market Tracker , HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami explains why a path to sub-7% mortgage rates is back on the table. While weekly pending home sales have recently stabilized, that doesn't yet signal a sustained recovery. For housing professionals, the opportunity is to translate those national trends into what clients are experiencing in their own markets. HousingWire Data from Houston, Phoenix and Tampa reveals three things worth watching: Look beyond the headline. A national or regional trend may not reflect the competition your client faces. Watch how the signals move together. Changes in pending sales, inventory and price reductions can reveal where competition may be heading. Recognize when conditions are shifting. Recent market activity can change before the longer-term numbers tell the same story. Look beyond the headline A client sees that housing demand is stabilizing and asks whether it's finally a good time to sell. Houston demonstrates why the answer requires more local context. Across the Houston metro, the ratio of new pending sales to new listings improved during October, but not because buyer activity increased. New listings declined faster than pending sales, making the ratio look stronger even as fewer homes went under contract. Within Houston city limits, the opposite happened. Pending sales declined faster than new listings, pushing the ratio lower. Even inventory told a different story. Active inventory was higher than a year ago across the metro but lower within the city. Neither market showed growing pending activity, yet the conditions affecting buyers and sellers were different. For a homeowner, that distinction matters more than whether a regional headline describes the market as improving. The takeaway: Use broader housing trends to start the conversation, then show clients what's happening among the homes they're actually competing with. A seller needs to understand current competition and buyer activity, not simply whether the overall market appears stronger. Watch how the signals move together A homeowner considering whether to wait for lower mortgage rates might assume that more affordable financing will bring more buyers. But lower rates could also encourage more sellers to list, making the relationship between supply and demand especially important. Phoenix illustrates what happens when several indicators point in the same direction. Over the latest four-week period, new pending sales declined faster than new listings. Compared with a year ago, pending activity was down nearly 17%, while new listings were slightly higher. Meanwhile, active inventory continued to grow, and more than half of active listings had experienced a price reduction. Together, those indicators suggest increasing competition among sellers. Fewer homes are moving into pending status, more inventory is available and price reductions are becoming more prevalent. That doesn't guarantee prices will fall, but it identifies conditions that could create additional pricing pressure if the trend continues. The takeaway: Don't evaluate pending sales, inventory or price reductions in isolation. When several indicators reinforce one another, they provide stronger evidence of where conditions may be headed. That can help sellers evaluate pricing and timing, while giving buyers a clearer picture of their negotiating position. Recognize when conditions are shifting A seller points out that inventory is still lower than last year. Does that mean competition remains limited? Tampa shows why the direction of recent activity matters just as much as the year-over-year comparison. Within Tampa city limits, new listings and pending sales were essentially unchanged over the latest four weeks. Active inventory remained below last year's level, and the share of listings with price reductions had declined. But inventory was also beginning to increase compared with the preceding four weeks. That doesn't establish a market shift. Recent pending activity has been relatively steady, and price-cut share continues to ease. Still, the inventory increase is worth monitoring. If inventory continues building while pending activity remains weak, sellers could face greater competition even before the year-over-year inventory comparison turns positive. The six-month view shows how inventory has been building recently, while the year-over-year comparison reveals that inventory remains below last year's levels. Both are true, but each tells you something different about the market. The takeaway: A favorable market statistic doesn't mean conditions are standing still. Track recent changes alongside year-over-year trends, and revisit pricing or buying strategies when the evidence begins to shift. Your clients can find national headlines and AI-generated market summaries on their own. What they need from you is the expertise to explain what those trends mean for their home, their competition and their next decision. items.title: Ballot roulette: Florida voters pick property tax break over local services
items.description: With the cost of living on the ballot, Florida voters approved a major tax break for homeowners. The amendment to increase the Sunshine State's homestead exemption won the 60% it needed on election night. Voters weren't swayed by warnings that the higher exemption would devastate municipal coffers and services. The ballot measure was given little chance of winning. But current economic conditions proved an insurmountable obstacle for the argument against the measure. Unofficial returns showed it finishing with 62% of the vote. The changes take effect in phases starting in 2027. "An incredible victory for Florida homeowners!" the Florida Republican Party wrote on social media . "More money stays in your pocket." Neil Schiller, managing partner at Government Law Group , told HousingWire TBD the result will change how cities weigh development. "Projects that generate jobs, economic activity, and alternative tax revenues may become more attractive, while developments that require significant public services and infrastructure will face greater financial scrutiny," Schiller said. "Amendment 3 may be remembered as the moment Florida cities had to fundamentally reinvent how they do business." The vote shows how important affordability has become, Andrew Hellinger, co-principal at Urban-X Group , developer of River Landing Shops & Residences in Miami, said in an e-mail to HousingWire TBD . Hellinger added, "However, people still need roads, public transportation and essential community services, and those have to be paid for." What the exemption does The amendment replaces the $50,000 homestead exemption with a phased increase. It rises to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Only primary residences qualify, so second-home and investment-property owners get nothing. Homeowners must establish Florida residency by Dec. 31, 2026, to get the full benefit. Later arrivals get the $50,000 exemption for four years before qualifying. The school board levy is excluded. The measure also cuts the annual assessment cap on non-homestead commercial property from 10% to 5%. That change starts Jan. 1, 2027. Renters, who occupy about a third of Florida's housing units, get no relief. How Florida got here Gov. Ron DeSantis called a special session to put the amendment on the ballot. Lawmakers approved it with changes protecting school funding. DeSantis had sought a broader exemption. DeSantis cast the measure as a fix for tax bills inflated by pandemic-era migration. Newcomers, led by New Yorkers, overwhelmed the housing supply and lifted values and tax burdens for longtime residents. Florida home prices rose more than 50% between 2020 and 2022. Prices have since stalled, and the average home value fell 3.7% over the past year. Assessments haven't followed: under the Save Our Homes recapture rule, they keep rising until they meet market value. The annual increase is capped at 3% or inflation, whichever is less. Most counties held millage rates steady or cut them, yet bills still climbed. City tax bills statewide rose about 50% on average over several years. Voters heard the warnings The Florida Sheriffs Association said in August it was "significantly concerned." By mid-September, it was running ads featuring sheriffs from four counties. One said, "We want a tax cut too, but Amendment 3 is the wrong way to do it." Association President Billy Woods warned of fewer deputies, slower 911 response and more crime. Opponents also included the Florida State Fraternal Order of Police , Florida Professional Firefighters and Florida Fire Chiefs Association . The Florida League of Cities and Florida Association of Counties opposed it, citing too much uncertainty. According to the legislature's economic research office, estimated local governments would lose nearly $5 billion in 2027-28. The Florida Policy Institute, a progressive think tank, created Floridians for Shared Prosperity, which sponsored a campaign urging a no vote. "Amendment 3 will leave working families and seniors with a lose-lose choice: pay more through new fees and higher taxes or face major cuts to the services you depend on," the campaign’s website stated. Voters approved the amendment anyway, with encouragement from the Florida Realtors and others in real estate. “This is your one shot at real property tax relief,” apartment owner and investor Grant Washington wrote on social media Monday. “Vote Yes on Amendment 3 and put your money back where it belongs. In your pocket!” Related More: Florida Property Tax

items.title: LGI Homes Q3 2026 earnings reveal leadership test in downturn
items.description: A peculiar phenomenon in homebuilding has fascinated me for much of the past two-plus decades. In virtually every market, across almost every customer segment and price point, a handful of homebuilders consistently outperform competitors facing essentially the same business conditions. They face the same mortgage rates, land and development costs, labor constraints, household purchasing-power challenges and regulatory obstacles. They work with essentially the same raw materials, including people, capital, building products, subcontractors and operating processes. Yet their results can differ dramatically, especially when business conditions turn difficult. A decade or so ago, a highly regarded homebuilding business strategist mused aloud to me about this phenomenon. He was struck by how companies dealt with essentially the same competitive hand, yet a few outlier leaders figured out how to produce better results than the rest. I've thought about that observation often, particularly during periods when the industry's cyclical pressures expose the difference between companies that can withstand adversity and those that can turn adversity into an opportunity to strengthen their businesses. The distinction is especially relevant now. U.S. homebuilders are facing an unforgiving mix of weak selling conditions, elevated capital costs, stubbornly high land and development expenses, and households whose purchasing power has failed to keep pace with the cost of homeownership. These pressures have persisted long enough to strain business plans based on more favorable assumptions, and little is certain about when conditions will improve. Which brings us to LGI Homes , its Q3 2026 earnings report, and a question that extends well beyond a single company's quarterly performance: What distinguishes homebuilding enterprises whose leaders and organizations can emerge from a prolonged downturn stronger than they entered it? LGI's third quarter: A revealing contradiction LGI Homes' November 3 earnings report is a useful case study because its operating results show both encouraging evidence of management's execution and unmistakable signs that the business faces tough sledding ahead. The Woodlands, Texas-based builder reported 1,222 home closings in the third quarter, including 33 currently or previously leased homes, a 10.4% increase from the year-earlier quarter. Homebuilding revenues rose 10.3% to $437.5 million, and net income increased to $24.6 million, or $1.05 per diluted share, compared with $19.7 million, or $0.85 per share, in the year-earlier quarter. Profitability and expense management emerged as clear strengths. Homebuilding gross margin reached 20.2%, and adjusted homebuilding gross margin was 23.7%, both up 40 basis points sequentially. Selling, general and administrative expenses declined 2.5% in absolute dollars, while SG&A as a percentage of total revenue improved 180 basis points year over year, reflecting operational rigor and executional excellence. The company also reduced its net debt-to-capital ratio to 40.6%, up 420 basis points from a year earlier, and ended September with $447.7 million in liquidity. Its active community count increased by 7.1% year over year to 151. Yet a forward-looking lens tells a far less rosy story. Net orders plunged 61.2% to 609 homes, down from 1,570 a year earlier, while the cancellation rate rose to 53.8% from 33.6%. Backlog declined 47.5% to 685 homes. Management narrowed its full-year closing guidance to 4,600 to 4,800 homes, reflecting weaker sales activity and ongoing affordability pressures. These results speak of the vulnerability of LGI's business model at a time when the company's core customer is among the most financially constrained in the housing market. LGI has built much of its business around helping renters become homeowners through a direct-to-consumer sales model, speculative construction, and a value proposition that emphasizes attainable monthly payments. These capabilities have helped distinguish the company for years. They also leave its sales performance especially vulnerable to turbulent headwinds, such as mortgage-rate movements and changes in buyer qualification. The third-quarter numbers make it clear that LGI's operational strengths have not shielded it from those pressures. Will the capabilities that helped the company develop its distinctive business model now enable it to adapt more effectively than competitors under the same conditions? Wall Street sees the strengths and the vulnerabilities Wolfe Research's November 3 assessment of LGI serves as an important counterweight to any temptation to interpret the company's earnings performance as evidence that it has already mastered the current downturn. Analyst Trevor Allinson and his team credited LGI's Q3 operating performance, namely its gross-margin strength and SG&A expense reductions, while maintaining a Peer Perform rating. Wolfe noted that LGI's predominantly self-developed land position supports margins at a time when several competitors have sustained hits to sequential margins. Wolf Research's analysis also explicitly recognizes LGI's process-driven organization as a competitive strength, citing the company's ability to pare back operating errors in land acquisition, construction efficiency and warranty management. This is not to say that Wall Street exactly overlooks the value of management execution or organizational capability. Wolfe's analysis shows that analysts recognize those strengths and attempt to account for their financial impact. items.title: U.S. REIT Omega Healthcare Investors Expands Care Home Platform In £615M Deal
items.description: Courtesy of Omega Healthcare Investors Omega Healthcare Investors is pledging to expand its UK care home platform. U.S. healthcare REIT Omega Healthcare Investors and Foundation Partners have acquired UK care home operator Runwood Homes in a £615M deal, adding 55 homes and 3,930 registered beds to their UK platform. The newly acquired homes will be operated by Evera Living, a new care platform established by Foundation Partners, which has partnered with Omega to invest in and grow the business. The companies said they are targeting further acquisitions in the UK care market. Evera Living will be led by John Forrest, formerly chief operating officer of Spire Healthcare, as CEO, with Vishul Seewoolall, previously COO of Signature Care and a regional operations director at Bupa, appointed COO. “Alongside Foundation Partners and Evera’s leadership, we see the opportunity to support a substantial UK care business with the capital and capabilities for its next chapter,” Omega Healthcare Investors Chief Investment Officer Vikas Gupta said in a statement. “The strength of this partnership is evergreen capital that shares our long-term perspective. Together, we want to build a multinational, multi-service care platform. We are thinking in decades, not towards a short-term exit,” Foundation Partners co-founder and Managing Partner Ben Puddle said. Omega, which has a global portfolio of approximately 1,100 care facilities, has been investing in the UK for several years, and its UK portfolio comprised approximately 300 facilities, with the Runwood acquisition taking its UK holdings beyond 350 care homes. Foundation Partners has invested approximately £750M in healthcare over the past decade and acquired and managed six operating platforms, representing more than 70 homes and 3,000 beds before the Runwood deal. Its previous investments include New Century Care, Hartford Care, Graham Care, Select Healthcare and Towerview Care. Runwood was founded by Gordon Sanders 40 years ago and has grown into one of the UK's larger elderly care operators. Knight Frank advised on the sale. items.title: D.C. Mayor-Elect Wants Options Beyond Therme's $550M Spa Proposal
items.description: D.C. Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George is keeping her options open for what could anchor Poplar Point, the District’s last major waterfront development opportunity. Lewis George won the mayoral race Tuesday night and is set to take the reins from Mayor Muriel Bowser, who will step down from her nearly 12-year run in January. Bowser’s administration has been pushing a proposal to anchor Poplar Point with a $550M thermal bathing retreat from Therme Group . On Wednesday, Lewis George said she doesn’t want to preclude other development opportunities that could better meet the needs of D.C. residents. “I don't want to foreclose proposals by declaring that Therme is what's going to be there,” she said at a press conference. “Therme is welcome to continue to try to be one of the anchors and partners there, but I don't want to move forward in foreclosing those opportunities.” Wikimedia Commons/Council of the District of Columbia Janeese Lewis George, photographed in September 2023 Poplar Point, a 110-acre parkland on the eastern bank of the Anacostia River, has long been envisioned as a future mixed-use waterfront neighborhood like Navy Yard or The Wharf. Over the past few years, the Bowser administration has accelerated efforts to kick-start the redevelopment project. And in 2025, it selected Therme as the anchor. Before Bowser's term ends, her administration has sought to finalize two key pieces of legislation that would move Poplar Point and Therme’s proposed spa forward. But Lewis George told The Washington Sun last month that she has concerns about the project and that the site should be used to build more affordable homes. The mayor-elect on Wednesday said the city “needs to put the people of the District of Columbia first” in all the deals it makes. “We want people to say, ‘Hey, we want to be on Poplar Point. We're willing to build X, Y and Z. We're willing to show up for the residents and give these many amenities,’” Lewis George said. She committed in her mayoral campaign to building 72,000 new homes , speeding up development of affordable homes and modernizing rent stabilization. She reiterated her pledge to focus on affordability and said she hopes to “show real impact” in her first year in office. “I feel confident that we can deliver on universal access to childcare, that we can rein in our utility companies and deliver more affordability as it relates to utilities for our city and, of course, that we can make it easier for people to build homes in the city, to build more homes so we can lower the cost,” she said. items.title: Deutsche Finance Offices Raided In Connection With BVK's U.S. Real Estate Investments
items.description: The offices of Deutsche Finance in Munich were raided by the Munich Public Prosecutor’s office as part of an investigation involving massive losses on a U.S. real estate portfolio into which Bayerische Versorgungskammer , the German pension fund better known as BVK, poured nearly $2B. Unsplash/Compagnons Deutsche Finance confirmed the raid was carried out on Tuesday in a brief statement that says it was searched as a “third party” to the case, that it was cooperating with authorities and that it “has been in contact with them for some time.” Deutsche Finance America filed a lawsuit in September against BVK in Delaware Superior Court for breach of contract, defamation, deceptive trade practices and a host of other claims related to its alleged mismanagement of the real estate porfolio that led to more than $1B in losses. BVK invested $1.9B in seven projects through a partnership with Deutsche Finance America and developer Michael Shvo , whose real estate empire has been battered by lawsuits and shed its core assets. The portfolio included San Francisco’s Transamerica Pyramid , which Shvo 's eponymous development firm sold for $691M in April at a loss for the ownership group that had poured more than $1B into the iconic tower. Shvo also sold the site of the historic Raleigh Hotel in Miami Beach in October 2025 after a plan to rehabilitate and redevelop the property into a $2B project collapsed amid poor sales . Other Shvo projects, like a Mandarin Oriental condo tower in Manhattan, drew high-profile complaints at the same time that the developer was engaged in a scathing legal battle with private club operator Core Club over a planned location in the Transamerica Pyramid. BVK, Germany’s largest pension fund, said in February that its total losses from the investments with Shvo exceeded $1B and that it was looking to exit its relationship with the developer. Other assets in the portfolio included the Mandarin Oriental Residences in Beverly Hills and the Coca-Cola building in Manhattan. In its September lawsuit, Deutsche Finance alleged that BVK’s mismanagement of the U.S. portfolio included failing to provide oversight on operating budgets, refinancing decisions and proposed leases. BVK misled Deutsche Finance about its involvement in the investments and hid that it controlled leasing, construction, financing, pricing and capital decisions at the projects, the suit says. BVK firmly rejected the allegations at the time and said they constituted “an obvious attempt by Deutsche Finance to divert attention from its own responsibility and its numerous, publicly known challenges.” The losses at BVK have drawn attention across Germany, including from investigators, Bloomberg reported . The pension fund oversees $137B in retirement assets for 2.8 million people. items.title: Retirees, not refis: FOA's 24% growth maps the next market
items.description: Retirees, not refis: FOA's 24% growth maps the next market By Colin McNamara Published November 04, 2026, 3:58 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Expert Quote: "Higher rates affect borrower proceeds, but they do not eliminate our customers' need for financial flexibility in retirement." — Kristen Sieffert, President, Finance of America Supporting Data: Finance of America increased its funded volume by 24% year over year in the third quarter. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Reverse mortgage lender Finance of America continues to see its funded volume increase, signaling demand for home equity solutions remains strong in a high-rate environment . Processing Content Volume totaled $748 million in the third quarter, up 24% year over year and 2% from the second quarter , according to FOA's latest earnings release. Since CEO Graham Fleming and President Kristen Sieffert assumed their roles in 2023, the lender has expanded volumes by 20% on average each year, Fleming said on an earnings call Tuesday. The company's forward outlook points to more originations, even as the rest of the mortgage industry reaches a projected downturn. The Mortgage Bankers Association forecasted the forward market to shrink 5% against FOA's double-digit growth. "The difference is demand," Sieffert said on the call. "Ours is driven by retirement need, not refinancing incentives. Higher rates affect borrower proceeds, but they do not eliminate our customers' need for financial flexibility in retirement." Sieffert credited the lender's success to its broad product suite, which features home equity conversion mortgages, its HomeSafe first lien reverse mortgage and second lien reverse mortgage. All three products posted volume increases of 14%, 15% and 63% year over year. FOA also announced the line of credit version of HomeSafe Second will launch soon. The company plans to expand the suite further next year as it moves from a top reverse mortgage lender to a leader in home equity solutions for retirement as a whole, Sieffert said. "Each of our products serves a different homeowner need, and together, they give us multiple paths to growth even when pricing pressure affects individual products," she said. Multiple other companies have launched home equity products this year to try to capture some of this demand. Rocket Mortgage has updated its offerings over the past few years, and said on an earnings call last week its recapture efforts have benefitted the lender's home equity business . FOA's revenue troubles Despite the increased funded volume, FOA posted negative $58 million in total revenue, its first quarter in the red in nearly two years. The lender's net income also dropped to -$110 million from -$29 million in the second quarter of this year and third quarter of 2025, according to the release. On an adjusted basis, FOA totaled a net income of $6 million, or $0.28 per share, still well below the S&P Capital IQ Pro consensus estimate of $1.26 per share. The lender blamed the poor financial showing on lower revenue margins in its retirement solutions segment, which were impacted by the increase in benchmark rates during the quarter. items.title: How midterm outcome may shape housing bill follow-up, GSE reform
items.description: How midterm outcome may shape housing bill follow-up, GSE reform By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published November 04, 2026, 1:32 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Expert Quote: "I don't see them in the '27-28 years coming out of conservatorship," — Jennifer McGuiness-Lubbert, CEO, Pivot Financial What's at Stake: How much federal money and regulation gets directed toward initiatives that could save borrowers money or require more spending on servicing compliance. With a "blue wave" in Congress and lame-duck lawmakers headed toward a budget deadline, housing bill appropriations Democrats have favored will likely be one near-term mortgage-related priority, one speaker at an industry conference said Tuesday. "It is urgent that 'Road" be funded," Sam Valverde, a former housing official who is now managing director at Falcon Capital Advisors, told attendees at the IMN Mortgage Servicing Rights conference on Tuesday, referring to the 21st Century Road to Housing bill. Processing Content Housing executive orders from the Republican administration may slow, he speculated. "I think you'd want to see what the reset is within the White House around dealing with a new Congress," Valverde said. The administration has made some moves to distance itself from housing issues even before the midterms, with Trump letting the authorization of the housing bill pass but calling it a lower priority and not explicitly backing it. Donald Trump Jr.'s business partner Omeed Malik left Fannie Mae's board just before the election, according to a Securities and Exchange Commission filing. The midterms also could shape how housing agencies, which Democrats have called for more scrutiny of, approach existing EO directives. GSE implications For one, the latest EO calls for the Federal Housing Finance Agency to consider reducing government-sponsored enterprises' loan-level price adjustments for title-waiver-eligible loans, potentially helping lenders but resulting in prepayments investors could view as a risk. "If MSR investors and MBS investors start to understand that policy changes will create repayment activity they cannot anticipate, they're going to ask for an uncertainty premium," Valverde said, noting that the FHFA has discretion on whether to follow through with this. Broader GSE reform, including the possibility of a stock sale, also is something the mortgage industry and investors will be watching closely now because many analysts have indicated that they anticipated it to be on hold until after the midterms. Democrats have generally been less eager to remove the GSEs from conservatorship administratively than Republicans but have been involved in some past legal proposals for reform. Some speakers at the IMN event said that they were skeptical of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's recent statements about a stock sale potentially being on the roadmap for 2027 or 2028, when there is an extendable deadline for conservatorship ending. "Even he is questioning whether the shareholder restructuring is going to help homeowners if mortgage spreads widen in doing so," said Tim Roy, vice president, housing finance policy, at the Independent Community Bankers of America. Jennifer McGuiness-Lubbert, CEO of Pivot Financial, said because plans regarding whether or not to make a share offering or depart conservatorship have changed multiple times, she's skeptical of action. "Even if they were to sell a component of the holdings of the Treasury and take in additional investment dollars. I don't see them in the '27-28 years coming out of conservatorship," she said. Bose George, managing director of Keefe, Bruyette & Woods, said KBW has put 30% odds on the GSEs leaving conservatorship and the percentage could be lower. Capital deficiencies and senior preferred shares remain hurdles, and even though a stock offering does not require Congress, the election sweep "could just make things harder, where other parts of the agenda get tougher to push through," George said. Another federal impact experts have broadly forecast to emerge from the midterms could be more regulation of artificial intelligence. Watch for more AI rules During separate conference discussions about AI, panelists noted that Fannie Mae updated one of its planned 2027 regulatory directives for what the Trump administration has called "superintelligence" not long before the midterms. With it possible to use AI to handle up to 60% of loss mitigation tasks and some states already requiring disclosures and opt-outs around its use, servicers should be prepared for increased regulation, panelists said. "There's a lot that to unpack there from a regulatory environment that will probably only continue to heat up," said Joshua Bishop, chief operating officer, servicing, at Newrez. "You've got to have a good, strong AI governance process."
