items.title: The Renovation Cool-Off Is Here, but Delaying Certain Repairs Could Cost You More Than You Save
items.description: Spending on home improvements and repairs is only expected to grow by 1.5% by the third quarter of 2027 , according to Harvard University Joint Center for Housing Studies. Given the high cost of labor and materials these days, this is no surprise. But if you’re trying to cut back on home projects to save some cash, it's important to understand which ones are truly optional and which ones actually need immediate attention. “Not every project needs to happen right away. Your home doesn't have to look brand-new to be safe, comfortable, and in good shape,” says Jeri Goodkin Dausey , president and certified general contractor at SBC in Miami Beach, FL . By knowing how to prioritze your budget, you can protect your home ’s condition and value without draining your savings. Projects you can safely delay There are quite a few projects you can delay without hurting your home, as long as everything is safe and working properly. “Sometimes, waiting can save you quite a bit of money in the short term,” Dausey explains. Here’s what you can put on the back burner until you have more funds at your disposal. Loading... Contractors working on a kitchen are a lot more expensive than they once were. Realtor.com/Getty Images Kitchen and bathroom makeovers If your cabinets, countertops, and fixtures are still in decent shape and everything works, there's no need to rush into a complete remodel. “Let's say you were planning to spend $25,000 on a renovation but could take care of the immediate issue with a $500 repair instead. That's $24,500 you can hold onto for now,” says Dausey. Painting and decorative updates A fresh coat of paint or new trim can make a significant difference in your home’s aestehtics, but these are usually things that can wait if the walls and surfaces are in good shape. “If you put off a $4,000 paint job and just spend $200 on a few touch-ups, you've kept another $3,800 in your budget,” Dausey explains. Dmitri Popescu , general manager at Olympic Decks in Seattle , echoes Dausey’s thoughts. “Repainting a room because you dislike the color or replacing an undamaged backsplash can generally wait. There’s no need to spend your money on a temporary makeover,” Popescu explains. Replacing floors just because they're dated Not loving the look of your floors doesn't necessarily mean you need to replace them. If they're safe, stable, and free of water damage, you may be able to live with them a little longer. “Putting off an $8,000 replacement and spending $300 on maintenance leaves you with $7,700. Just be sure to check out loose tiles, soft spots or areas that are lifting,” says Dausey. Outdoor extras and upgrades An outdoor kitchen, new landscaping, or a bigger patio might be nice to have, but they're not necessities. If everything outside is safe and in good shape, these projects can wait. “Delaying a $15,000 cosmetic upgrade in your backyard frees up a lot of money for other things. Just don't overlook problems like poor drainage, hazardous trees, or an unsafe deck,” advises Dausey. Loading... Repairing an electric water heater is necessary but expensive. Getty Images How to determine what to put off These expert tips can help you decide whether a project can wait: Be honest about the purpose of the project Ask yourself, does this project actually protect my home, or is it simply for aesthetics? “Cosmetic upgrades can wait, but projects that protect the structural integrity and long-term value of your property can't,” says Roxanne Conrad , chief operating officer at Premium Service Brands in Charlottesville, VA . Determine if cold weather will exacerbate the problem Clogged gutters and unstable exterior surfaces like missing shingles and unsealed windows, for example, can be an issue. “They can lead to much larger problems down the road if neglected for too long,” Conrad says. Acknowledge how long the issue has been around If you’ve noticed the issue a while ago and it’s worsening, it likely deserves your time and money. “Catching problems early is almost always easier and cheaper than repairing them as they fail,” Conrad explains. Remember that not everything needs to be done at once Take care of what keeps your home safe, dry, and in good shape, and don't feel pressured to tackle every cosmetic project right away. Keith Ostendorf , project developer at Next Stage Design + Build in San Jose, CA , recommends phasing. “Some homeowners move forward in phases, which spreads out the spending and can cut the costs of moving out, since work in one part of the house can happen while the family lives in the rest,” he adds.

items.title: JD Vance Blames Iran War for GOP Rout as Mortgage Rates Soared
items.description: Vice President JD Vance is blaming Republicans' election losses on the Iran conflict and rising prices. "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance said in a post on X, hours after Democrats shellacked Republicans in the midterm elections , flipping almost three dozen seats in the House and Senate to win control of both chambers. Vance noted that polling found the war in Iran and cost of living and inflation concerns were the top items on voters' minds heading into Election Day. Those were among the top reasons that many of the voters who helped propel President Donald Trump to a second term in 2024, with majorities in both chambers of Congress, voted in Democrats on Tuesday, Vance said. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance said in the post. "The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," Vance said. Indeed, Americans were broadly concerned about affordability in the months leading up to the election. While Trump said he remained focused on it, he spent the run-up to the election detailing projects in Washington, DC, such as a botched effort to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool . Both Democrats and Republicans have promised their own affordability agendas for the coming months. But in swing states that turned against Trump , including Iowa , Ohio , Texas , and Maine , housing affordability was at the top of voters' minds. So, too, have many young voters worried that homeownership is rising out of reach . Inflation worries Most markers of inflation show many costs have risen sharply this year. Gas prices often embody Americans' concerns, and AAA reports the national average price for gas is $4.12 a gallon, compared to $3.05 a year ago. Trump, for his part, continued defending his economic record on Tuesday, telling media outlets that night that he would accept the election results and might seek common ground with Democrats. But then he also posted an image of a red hat with the word "veto" on it, before celebrating the rise of the Dow the next morning following the results. "Stock Market just hit another Record High—91 Days in just a short period of time—Less than two years," he posted to Truth Social on Wednesday. "Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All!" And yet, the war in Iran and its resultant rise in oil prices and other costs hamstrung efforts to improve affordability. The Federal Reserve hiked interest rates earlier this year, and kept them steady in its most recent meeting. Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee in recent months show that leaders are worried that inflation is stickier than expected and that the conflict with Iran will continue to drive up costs. Vance said in his post that it was "sound" political advice to call for a diplomatic solution to the Iran conflict. He also indicated that he could be open for change to the controversial immigration enforcement policies that have deeply affected the housing market and home construction. "I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance," Vance said in the post. "But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you." Democrats take aim at affordability Meanwhile, Democratic leaders said in a press conference on Wednesday that they would focus on affordability in the coming term. Loading... "We're going to fight hard for the heartland of America," New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is likely to become the new Speaker of the House, said on Wednesday. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries , who is likely to become the new Speaker of the House, repeatedly avoided discussing Trump. Instead, he said his focus was on "affordability and accountability." "We know we have to undertake, with the seriousness of purpose, a relentless effort to make life more affordable for everyday Americans," Jeffries said. Later he added, "We have been focused, relentlessly, on dealing with the affordability crisis and driving down the high cost of living." Massachusetts Rep. Katherine Clark , who is currently minority whip but stands as a contender to become House majority leader, said that could include efforts to roll back the president's tariffs , which have driven up the cost of many homebuilding materials and household goods . Jeffries said the House Democratic Caucus will convene next week and lay out a clear plan for what to do next. But neither he nor Sen. Chuck Schumer had heard directly from Trump on Wednesday. NAR calls for bipartisanship The National Association of Realtors®, in a Wednesday statement, called for more progress on housing. “Regardless of which party controls Congress, NAR’s priorities remain the same: increasing housing supply, improving affordability, protecting property rights and expanding access to homeownership," NAR said. "Our research shows that 85% of Americans believe homeownership is part of the American Dream, underscoring why housing must remain a priority for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle." RPAC-supported candidates won in at least 325 races, and a number of ballot initiatives this year involved housing-related issues . NAR also noted the bipartisanship of the 21st Century Road to Housing Act , the housing package aimed at making it easier to build homes. Congress passed it this summer with large majorities from both parties. "We will continue building on that momentum, working with REALTOR® champions and real estate allies in both parties to advance commonsense solutions that bring more homes to the market and help more Americans achieve the dream of homeownership," NAR said.
